assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore showed how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks. This is a foundational mechanism for credit cycles, and the Gertler line of work built it into quantitative macro models used in policy. The framework is widely taught and is central to understanding financial crises, including historical ones.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) are the clearest core credit. Gertler is the strongest third name through the financial-accelerator and quantitative intermediation work. Bernanke's earlier prize covers part of the accelerator lineage, so Gertler's marginal credit needs scrutiny. Gilchrist is a plausible but less central contributor.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The core papers date from the 1990s, and empirical and policy use is well established, including after 2008.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize for banking and crises (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) may reduce the perceived novelty.
Gertler also appears on the New Keynesian ballot entry, which complicates attribution across the two entries.
My assessment draws on general knowledge and has not been independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Melitz (2003) turned firm heterogeneity into the workhorse of modern trade theory. It explained selection, exporter premia and gains from trade beyond Krugman's new trade theory. Helpman and co-authors extended it to firm-level trade patterns, offshoring and labour-market outcomes. The work has large empirical and policy reach.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the central originator. Helpman has broad foundational and extension credit. Redding's contributions are significant, especially on quantitative and spatial trade, but are more recent and cumulative. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on this entry and are relevant to the empirical foundations.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Two decades of replication, extension and quantitative application, and the framework is standard.
uncertainties: The trade field has several competing entries (B020, B046), and committee judgment on which agenda is more fundamental may differ.
Priority questions relative to the empirical firm-level evidence not credited on this entry.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Founded modern political economics with a systematic framework for how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and development. It combines formal theory with empirical identification and has opened a field now widely used across economics and political science. The state-capacity strand ties directly to long-run development and historical evidence.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the core originators, including their joint book and the constitutional-rules papers. Besley's contributions on state capacity, accountability and development are substantial and often joint with Persson. Acemoglu and Robinson already share the 2024 prize on institutions, so the committee must distinguish this agenda.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The agenda has been developed for three decades with strong empirical follow-up.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity may shape how the committee judges novelty.
Careful delimitation of three names among a broad literature is needed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reconstructed long-run top-income and wealth series from tax data, changing the empirical basis of inequality debates. It had large influence on public economics, economic history and policy. Methodological contributions are real, but some theoretical and interpretive claims are contested.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez built the top-incomes series jointly. Zucman's wealth and offshore-wealth work is important and more recent. Atkinson, who has died, is not eligible. Credit is also shared with many collaborators and a wider network of national top-income databases.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature for the income-series work. Debate persists on the wealth-concentration conclusions and on methods for wealth estimation.
uncertainties: Contested interpretation of capital-in-the-twenty-first-century arguments may weigh against Piketty.
The most robust contribution is data construction rather than a single theoretical result.
Whether Zucman should be included depends on a judgment about maturity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Used linked population administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility and its local determinants at unprecedented scale. It changed how economists measure opportunity and evaluate place-based and policy effects. Methodological and empirical reach is very large.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the intellectual leader and principal author on the major papers. Hendren (neighbourhood effects) and Friedman (mobility and teacher value-added) are key co-authors. Katz contributes through earlier work on Moving to Opportunity. Credit is clearly team-based.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. Some results (neighbourhood and exposure effects) are well replicated, while others are recent and still being assessed.
uncertainties: Time may be needed to establish long-run validity and policy durability.
The team-based nature of the work complicates the three-name limit.
Chetty's broader portfolio (taxation, B044) may also affect framing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Established, theoretically and experimentally, that fairness, reciprocity and inequity aversion shape behaviour and contract design. Fehr-Schmidt (1999) gave a tractable model of social preferences, and Fehr's experiments on strong reciprocity and punishment broadened the empirical base. The work is influential in behavioural, public and organisational economics.
assessment.attribution: Fehr is the central figure across experiments and theory. Schmidt shares the formal inequity-aversion model. Falk's contributions concern field evidence and preferences, and he is a plausible but less central third name. Bolton and Ockenfels (ERC) are not credited and offered a close contemporaneous model.
assessment.maturity: Mature. Over twenty-five years of replication, though debates on external validity and on stability of preferences continue.
uncertainties: Behavioural economics has already been recognised several times (Kahneman, Thaler), which may reduce the available space.
Concerns about laboratory generalisability and the contemporaneous Bolton-Ockenfels model.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the trade-shock evidence changed understanding of how automation and import competition reshape labour demand, wages and regional outcomes. The topic is highly policy-relevant, and the work links to long-run questions about how societies adjust to technological change. Empirical designs are influential, though some interpretations are debated.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the main contributor across task and trade-shock strands. Hanson and Dorn are central to the China-shock papers. Katz has deep earlier credit on skill-biased change (partly with Goldin, who has a prize). Acemoglu has the 2024 prize and shares the task framework with Autor, which complicates attribution.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. The task framework is well established, while the long-run consequences of the China shock are still being studied.
uncertainties: The overlap with Acemoglu's recognised work on technology and tasks makes the incremental credit hard to separate.
Some effects of the China shock are contested in terms of persistence and magnitude.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Showed that misallocation of inputs across firms can account for a large share of cross-country income differences, giving a measurable, tractable link between micro-level distortions and aggregate productivity. The paper launched a large literature in macro-development and growth, with policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) are the core pair. Restuccia and Rogerson (not credited) have close parallel contributions, and Restuccia is credited here, so attribution is contested and Restuccia is a credible alternative third name.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature. About fifteen years of use, but the measurement of misallocation from revenue productivity is debated, because measurement error and markups can confound it.
uncertainties: Measurement criticisms could weaken the empirical claims.
Credit to Restuccia and Rogerson complicates the choice of names.
A recipient may be more plausible after further validation.
